label: cor:ftc_eval
title: Evaluation of integrals via antiderivatives
statement:
Let $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[\min(a,b), \max(a,b)]$ and let $F$ be an antiderivative of $f$ on $(\min(a,b), \max(a,b))$ that is continuous on $[\min(a,b), \max(a,b)]$. Then
    \[
      \int_a^b f(x)\,dx = F(b) - F(a).
    \]
proof: By the First FTC (Theorem~\ref{thm:ftc1}), the function $G(u) = \int_a^u f(t)\,dt$ is also an antiderivative of $f$ on the interior. Then $F - G$ has zero derivative on the interior, so by Lemma~\ref{lem:zero_deriv_constant}, $F(x) - G(x)$ is constant on $[\min(a,b), \max(a,b)]$. In particular $F(b) - G(b) = F(a) - G(a)$, which gives $G(b) - G(a) = F(b) - F(a)$. Since $G(a) = \int_a^a f = 0$, we get $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = F(b) - F(a)$. Alternatively, if $F$ has right derivatives, this follows directly from the Second FTC (Theorem~\ref{thm:ftc2}).
